newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Pemex sees placing $900 mln debt in 97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Pemex sees placing $900 mln debt in 97.

text.p: Mexico's state-owned oil giant Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) sees placing debt issues worth up to a total of $900 million next year, said Pemex's chief financial officer, Juan Manuel Romero.
The company, the world's fifth biggest crude producer, does not plan to go to the debt markets again this year, after already placing three issues worth almost $800 million.

In the coming year Pemex also plans to extend the maturities on its debt, moving to medium-term paper from the two- and three-year maturities it placed this year, Romero said in an interview with Reuters.
"I don't believe that for the rest of 1996 that we will be placing another issue. We are not going to place another issue," Romero said.
Debt issues next year will be similar to this year, when Pemex placed three bonds, only the company will aim to extend the tenor of its debt, he noted.
"We are looking at an upper limit of $900 million (in 1997) against the almost $800 million that we placed this year," he said.

"For the $900 million that we see in the coming year, we could start the process early in 1997. For me, the best time would be the month of March, when we have the results for 1996, which will be extraordinary good," he said.
"We will be looking, if we make bond issues, to placements of five to seven years," he added.
Pemex, for the most part, shied away from capital markets in 1995 after the economic crash, thinking that the premium demanded on Mexican debt issues was too high.
But in 1996 the oil giant placed three issues in the Euromarket, the first a two-year issue in March for about $192.6 million worth of Italian lira.

In June, it launched a two-year issue worth $300 million with yield of 190 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. In October it placed another $300 million in Euronotes, this time for three-years, with a spread of 175 basis points over Treasuries.
Next year, the oil giant expects to place about half its issues in the Yankee market, which they consider highly important.
"We are anticipating that about half of the $900 million that we will be placing will be in the American market," Romero said, adding the rest would likely be in the Euromarket.
Pemex has an aggressive investment program in 1997, he noted, but much of the funding will be generated internally.
The company has benefited from strong prices for its oil, from cost cutting and from production increases, which will lead to "extraordinarily" better results for 1996, he said.
But the company will be looking for project funding, in large part tied to four important projects.
Project funding needs for next year will be about $2.0 billion, he said.
For 1998, Pemex sees fulfilling these financing needs in an "aggressive" mannner, as work on several of the projects that intensified in 1997 will reach an funding peak in 1998, he said.
"We see 1998 as a year even more aggressive in terms of financing," he said.
The unknown is how much money Pemex will be able to generate itself in 1998, which is tied to demand for its product and the price of oil.
"But of course, if the conditions are there, it is certainly possible that we could have bigger incursions into capital markets," he said.
Romero is expecting spreads on Mexican debt, and on Pemex's, to decrease as the economic recovery and growth in Mexico strengthens.
